hints: Picture the two forms of 2-aminobutane in a mirror and ask whether you could lay one exactly on top of the other.
walkthrough:
See the chiral centre in 2-aminobutane**
Look at carbon 2 in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. It is bonded to four different groups: $\text{H}$, $\text{NH}_{2}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. That makes it a chiral centre, so two different 3D arrangements are possible.

Link mirror images to the definition**
Those two arrangements are mirror images, just like left and right hands. Because the four groups are all different, no rotation will make one fit exactly on top of the other. That non-superimposable mirror image relationship is exactly what the word enantiomers means.
Final answer: Enantiomers are a pair of stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

hints: Focus on the nitrogen atom in the $\text{-NH}_{2}$ group and recall what feature all amines use to act as bases.
Think about what happens when that feature interacts with water and which ion causes pH greater than 7.
walkthrough:
Spot why an amine is basic**
Do not think of an amine as releasing $\text{OH}^{-}$ directly. Think Bronsted-Lowry base. The nitrogen in $\text{-NH}_{2}$ has a lone pair that can be donated to a proton, $\text{H}^{+}$. That is the key basic site.

Write the reaction with water**
In water, 2-aminobutane removes $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$:
$$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{3}^{+})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{OH}^{-}$$
Formation of $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions makes $[\text{OH}^{-}] > [\text{H}^{+}]$, so pH is greater than 7.

Final answer: The lone pair on N accepts a proton / $\text{H}^{+}$ from water, forming $\text{OH}^{-}$.
$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{3}^{+})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{OH}^{-}$

hints: Compare the groups attached to N in diethylamine, $(\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2})_{2}\text{NH}$, with those in 2-aminobutane, a primary amine.
Recall how alkyl groups push electron density toward nitrogen and what this does to the lone pair.
walkthrough:
Count the alkyl groups on nitrogen**
2-aminobutane is a primary amine with essentially one alkyl group directly influencing the $\text{-NH}_{2}$ nitrogen. Diethylamine, $(\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2})_{2}\text{NH}$, is a secondary amine with two ethyl groups bonded directly to N.

Connect donation to basicity**
Alkyl groups are electron donating by the inductive effect. They push electron density onto N. With two ethyl groups, the nitrogen in diethylamine becomes more electron rich, so its lone pair is more readily donated to $\text{H}^{+}$. That means a greater extent of reaction with water, more $\text{OH}^{-}$ formed at the same concentration, and therefore a higher pH.

Final answer: Diethylamine has two electron-donating alkyl / ethyl groups on N, whereas 2-aminobutane has only one alkyl chain attached to N.
The extra electron donation increases electron density on N, making the lone pair more available to accept $\text{H}^{+}$, so diethylamine is a stronger base and gives higher $[\text{OH}^{-}]$ and higher pH.

hints: Remember that a carboxylic acid transfers a proton to an amine without eliminating water, so think salt, not amide.
walkthrough:
Recognise proton transfer, not condensation**
With ethanoic acid at room temperature, the secondary amine simply acts as a base. The $\text{-COOH}$ donates $\text{H}^{+}$ to the nitrogen lone pair. No water is lost, so no amide forms yet.
$$\text{(CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{)}_{2}\text{NH} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{(CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{)}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}^{+} \text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$$
The product is diethylammonium ethanoate, an ionic salt.

hints: Think about nucleophilic attack by the amine nitrogen on the $\text{C=O}$ carbon of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ and what small molecule is expelled.
walkthrough:
Build the substituted amide**
The lone pair on N attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethanoyl chloride and $\text{Cl}$ leaves as $\text{HCl}$. Because the starting amine is secondary, the nitrogen in the product is bonded to two ethyl groups plus the acyl group:
$$\text{(CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{)}_{2}\text{NH} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CON(CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2} + \text{HCl}$$
This is $N,N$-diethylethanamide, a tertiary amide.

hints: Check each monomer for a $\text{C=C}$ double bond versus two different functional groups that can lose a small molecule.
walkthrough:
Sort by functional group pattern**
$\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(CH}_{3}\text{)COOH}$ contains a $\text{C=C}$ bond, so it joins by addition polymerisation with no small molecule lost. The benzene monomer has an acyl chloride $\text{-COCl}$ at one end and an alcohol $\text{-OH}$ at the other, and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)COOH}$ has $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COOH}$. Both are bifunctional monomers that link with loss of $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, so both undergo condensation polymerisation.

hints: Identify the new link formed between $\text{-COOH}$ of ethanedioic acid and $\text{-NH}_{2}$ of the diamine and draw it displayed as $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$.
Combine one full diacid residue with one full diamine residue to make one repeat unit, adding continuation bonds at each end.
walkthrough:
Form the two amide links**
Each $\text{-COOH}$ of $\text{HOOC-COOH}$ reacts with an $\text{-NH}_{2}$ of $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, losing $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to give $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$. You must display the amide linkage fully, showing $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ explicitly, not just writing CONH.

Assemble one repeat unit**
Take the whole diacid fragment plus the whole diamine fragment:
$$\text{-C(=O)-C(=O)-NH-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-NH-}$$
Put continuation bonds through the left hand carbonyl carbon and the right hand nitrogen to show the chain continues. This represents only one repeat unit of polymer W, a polyamide.

Final answer: One repeat unit of polyamide W with displayed amide groups and continuation bonds:
$\text{-C(=O)-C(=O)-NH-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-NH-}$
where both $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ are shown displayed and bonds continue through the outer $\text{C}$ and $\text{N}$ atoms.

hints: Compare the all carbon backbone of a poly(alkene) with the polar $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-N}$ bonds in polyamides and polyesters.
walkthrough:
See why there is no point of attack**
Poly(alkenes) such as poly(ethene) contain only strong, non-polar $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ single bonds. There is no polar carbonyl or other functional group for water or bacterial enzymes to attack by hydrolysis. That chemical inertness means micro-organisms cannot easily break the long chains, so biodegradation is very slow.
Final answer: Poly(alkenes) have a non-polar C-C backbone that is chemically inert and difficult to hydrolyse by water or enzymes.
